```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse   = TRUE,
  comment    = "#>",
  message    = FALSE,
  warning    = FALSE,
  fig.width  = 9,
  fig.height = 5,
  out.width  = "100%"
)
```

This walkthrough runs ReportR from start to finish on `sgpData_LONG`, a
simulated statewide data set from the SGPdata package. It holds five years
(2020–2024) of reading and mathematics results for grades 3–10, about 366,000
student test records. Every table, plot, and narrative on this page was
produced by the code shown, and the whole walkthrough runs in about a minute.

You will:

1. [Prepare the student records](#prepare-the-student-records)
2. [Describe the assessment](#describe-the-assessment)
3. [Run the general trend analysis](#run-the-general-trend-analysis) and look inside the results
4. [Check score quality](#check-score-quality)
5. [Run the other lines of analysis](#run-the-other-lines-of-analysis)
6. [Save the results and export tables](#save-the-results-and-export-tables)
7. [Render a report](#render-a-report)

The last section, [Adapting ReportR to your state](#adapting-reportr-to-your-state),
lists what changes when you use your own data.

## Before you start

Install ReportR from GitHub and the SGPdata package from CRAN:

```{r install, eval = FALSE}
install.packages(c("devtools", "SGPdata", "openxlsx"))
devtools::install_github("ndadey/ReportR")
```

Then load the packages:

```{r libraries}
library(ReportR)
library(SGPdata)
library(dplyr)
```

## Prepare the student records

Every ReportR analysis reads one data frame, `student_results_long`, with one
row per student, year, and subject. Start from the raw records, keep the valid
cases, and standardize the column names:

```{r standardize}
student_results_long <- sgpData_LONG |>
  filter(VALID_CASE == "VALID_CASE") |>
  standardize_student_results()
```

`standardize_student_results()` renames common source columns to the names
ReportR expects. Columns keep their positions, so comparing names side by side
shows what changed:

```{r renamed}
renamed <- names(sgpData_LONG) != names(student_results_long)

data.frame(
  original     = names(sgpData_LONG)[renamed],
  standardized = names(student_results_long)[renamed]
) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

It also converts academic-year labels to the year the test was given:

```{r years}
unique(sgpData_LONG$YEAR)
sort(unique(student_results_long$YEAR))
```

**Standardize before filtering by year.** Raw SGP-format data stores years as
text such as `"2019_2020"`, so a filter like `YEAR %in% 2022:2024` returns no
rows until the years have been converted.

### State-specific cleanup

Every state's data needs a little cleanup that no general function can
anticipate. This data needs two fixes:

- Some records have no scale score (achievement level `"No Score"`). They
  can't contribute to score analyses, so drop them.
- Yes/no flags carry a label prefix, for example `"ELL: Yes"` and
  `"IEP: No"`. School-level percentages count `Yes`, `Y`, `TRUE`, or `1` as
  "yes", so strip the prefix. Gender gets the same treatment so its values read
  `Female` and `Male`.

```{r cleanup}
student_results_long <- student_results_long |>
  filter(!is.na(SCALE_SCORE)) |>
  mutate(across(c(FRL, EL, IEP, GENDER), ~ sub("^.*: ", "", .x)))
```

Here are all of one student's records. The same `STUDENT_ID` appears in every
year the student was tested, which is what makes cohort analyses possible:

::: {.rr-scroll}
```{r peek}
one_student <- student_results_long$STUDENT_ID[1]

student_results_long |>
  filter(STUDENT_ID == one_student) |>
  arrange(SUBJECT, YEAR) |>
  select(STUDENT_ID, YEAR, SUBJECT, GRADE, SCALE_SCORE,
         ACHIEVEMENT_LEVEL, FRL) |>
  knitr::kable()
```
:::

## Describe the assessment

Everything specific to an assessment program lives in one R file, the
**assessment spec**. ReportR ships with a spec for this demo data. Sourcing it
creates a list called `assessment_spec`:

```{r spec}
source(system.file("specs/00_DEMO_Assessment_Spec.R", package = "ReportR"))
names(assessment_spec)
```

The spec names the achievement levels, from lowest to highest, and which level
counts as proficient:

```{r spec-levels}
assessment_spec$achievement_levels
```

For each subject and grade it records the lowest and highest obtainable scale
scores (LOSS and HOSS) and the cut scores between levels:

```{r spec-scores}
get_score_spec(assessment_spec, "MATHEMATICS", grade = 5)
```

Each cut is the highest score in the lower level, and a score's level is the
number of cuts it exceeds, plus one. A grade 5 mathematics score of 500 exceeds
the first two cuts (421 and 493), so it is level 3: Proficient.

The analysis code never hardcodes any of these values, so the same functions
work for a four-level or five-level assessment, and for end-of-course subjects
as well as grade-level ones. To describe your own assessment, copy the
template and fill it in:

```{r spec-template, eval = FALSE}
file.copy(
  system.file("specs/00_TEMPLATE_Spec.R", package = "ReportR"),
  "00_MyState_Assessment_Spec.R"
)
```

## Run the general trend analysis

Each line of analysis has one function that runs all of its sub-analyses.
Line 1, general trend, asks how performance has changed over time:

```{r trend}
general_trend_results <- run_general_trend_analysis(
  student_results_long = student_results_long,
  assessment_spec      = assessment_spec,
  min_n                = 10
)

names(general_trend_results)
```

Cells with fewer than `min_n` students have their statistics set to missing.
To limit the analysis to recent years, add `report_years = 2022:2024`.

### Inside the results

Each sub-analysis keeps its outputs together. Scale score trends, for example,
have a table, plots, and text:

```{r anatomy}
names(general_trend_results$score_trends)
```

**The table** has one row per subject and grade, with year-by-year means,
standard deviations, and counts. Here are the mathematics means:

```{r trend-table}
general_trend_results$score_trends$table |>
  filter(SUBJECT == "MATHEMATICS") |>
  select(GRADE, ends_with("_Mean")) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 1)
```

**The plots** are ggplot objects, one per subject for each plot type
(`mean_trend`, `mean_sd`, `median_iqr`, and `grade_profile`). Each grade's
panel spans that grade's score range:

```{r trend-plot, fig.height = 5.5}
general_trend_results$score_trends$plot$mean_trend$MATHEMATICS
```

**The narrative** is written from the results, so report text always matches
the numbers:

```{r trend-narrative-code, eval = FALSE}
cat(general_trend_results$score_trends$text$narrative)
```

::: {.rr-narrative}
```{r trend-narrative, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
cat(general_trend_results$score_trends$text$narrative)
```
:::

### Proficiency and achievement-level transitions

The proficiency sub-analysis tracks the percent of students at or above the
policy benchmark:

```{r proficiency-plot}
general_trend_results$proficiency$plot$trend
```

Achievement-level transitions follow the same students from one grade and year
to the next grade the following year, and show how often they moved up, stayed
at the same level, or moved down. In each grade's heatmap, a cell is the share
of all matched students who were at one level (row) and reached another level
(column) a year later, averaged across year pairs. The diagonal holds the
students who stayed at the same level:

```{r transitions-plot, fig.height = 9}
general_trend_results$achievement_transitions$matrices$plot$heatmap$MATHEMATICS
```

## Check score quality

Line 4 looks for patterns worth investigating before results are shared:
pileups at the floor or ceiling of the scale, scores outside the valid range,
unusual year-to-year changes, shifts in how strongly scores correlate across
years, and unusual distribution shapes.

```{r anomaly}
anomaly_results <- run_anomaly_analysis(student_results_long, assessment_spec)

names(anomaly_results)
```

The score integrity check compares every score with the spec. It flags scores
outside the LOSS–HOSS range, and achievement levels that disagree with the cut
scores:

```{r integrity-code, eval = FALSE}
cat(anomaly_results$score_integrity$text$narrative)
```

::: {.rr-narrative}
```{r integrity, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
cat(anomaly_results$score_integrity$text$narrative)
```
:::

That makes it a quick test of a new spec, too. Out-of-range scores or level
mismatches usually mean a score range or cut score in the spec is wrong.

The outlier check flags subject, grade, and year cells whose change from the
previous year is unusually large compared with the other cells:

```{r outliers-code, eval = FALSE}
cat(anomaly_results$outliers$text$narrative, sep = "\n\n")
```

::: {.rr-narrative}
```{r outliers-narrative, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
cat(anomaly_results$outliers$text$narrative, sep = "\n\n")
```
:::

```{r outliers-plot}
anomaly_results$outliers$plot$score
```

The correlation check follows the same students from one grade to the next.
Stable correlations across years suggest the scores rank students consistently:

```{r correlations}
anomaly_results$correlations$plot$line
```

## Run the other lines of analysis

The remaining lines work the same way: one function call, one results list.

### Enrollment (Line 1.2)

Who was tested, and how has the tested population changed?

```{r enrollment}
enrollment_results <- run_general_enrollment_analysis(
  student_results_long, assessment_spec
)

enrollment_results$counts$by_year |>
  select(YEAR, N, N_change, N_pct_change) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 1)
```

::: {.rr-narrative}
```{r enrollment-narrative, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
cat(enrollment_results$text$narrative)
```
:::

### Cohort (Line 1.3)

Cohort analysis follows the same students as they move through the grades,
which requires student IDs that persist across years. Each colored line is one
cohort, labeled by the year its students were (or would have been) in grade 3.
The dashed line shows all students tested in each grade, for comparison:

```{r cohort, fig.height = 5.5}
cohort_results <- run_cohort_analysis(student_results_long, assessment_spec)

cohort_results$plot$mean_scores$MATHEMATICS
```

`run_general_cohort()` runs the same analysis and also saves the results and
renders the cohort report in one step.

### School and district (Line 5)

The school and district line summarizes performance by school and district.
It also models each school's proficiency rate from its demographic composition
(the percent of students who are FRL, EL, IEP, and from minority groups), and
flags schools well above or below what the model predicts:

::: {.rr-scroll}
```{r aggregate}
aggregate_results <- run_aggregate_analysis(student_results_long, assessment_spec)

aggregate_results$outliers$positive_outlier_schools |>
  select(SUBJECT, YEAR, SCHOOL_NAME, n_tested, pct_proficient,
         predicted_proficiency, residual) |>
  head() |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 1)
```
:::

## Save the results and export tables

Save each results list once. Reports read the saved file, so you can revise and
render a report as often as you like without rerunning the analysis.

```{r save}
output_dir <- file.path(tempdir(), "reportr-demo")  # or any folder you choose
dir.create(output_dir, showWarnings = FALSE)

saveRDS(general_trend_results,
        file.path(output_dir, "general_trend_results.rds"))
```

`export_tables_to_excel()` writes every table in a results list to its own
worksheet, named after its place in the list:

```{r export}
xlsx_file <- file.path(output_dir, "general_trend_tables.xlsx")
export_tables_to_excel(general_trend_results, xlsx_file)

sheets <- openxlsx::getSheetNames(xlsx_file)
length(sheets)
head(sheets, 4)
```

## Render a report

Each line of analysis has a Quarto report template. Copy the template next to
your saved results, then render it with Quarto. The report reads the results
file and the spec, and writes a Word document:

```{r render, eval = FALSE}
file.copy(
  system.file("templates/01_General_Trend_Report.qmd", package = "ReportR"),
  output_dir
)

quarto::quarto_render(
  input          = file.path(output_dir, "01_General_Trend_Report.qmd"),
  output_format  = "docx",
  execute_params = list(
    spec_file    = system.file("specs/00_DEMO_Assessment_Spec.R",
                               package = "ReportR"),
    results_file = file.path(output_dir, "general_trend_results.rds"),
    report_years = 2022:2024
  )
)
```

Rendering requires [Quarto](https://quarto.org) and the `quarto` R package.
`report_years` limits the main tables to recent years. Leave it out to show
every year. The templates are ordinary Quarto documents, so edit your copy to
add state-specific context or change the layout.

| Line | Results from | Template |
|------|--------------|----------|
| 1. General trend | `run_general_trend_analysis()` | `01_General_Trend_Report.qmd` |
| 1.2 Enrollment | `run_general_enrollment_analysis()` | `01_Enrollment_Trends_Report.qmd`, `01_Enrollment_Brief.qmd` |
| 1.3 Cohort | `run_general_cohort()` | `01_General_Cohort_Report.qmd` |
| 4. Score quality | `run_anomaly_analysis()` | `04_Anomaly_Report.qmd` |
| 5. School and district | `run_aggregate_analysis()` | `05_Aggregate_Analysis_Report.qmd` |

## Adapting ReportR to your state

1. **Write a spec.** Copy `00_TEMPLATE_Spec.R` and fill in your subjects (their
   codes must match the `SUBJECT` values in your data), grades (`NULL` for
   end-of-course subjects), achievement levels, policy benchmark, score ranges,
   and cut scores. The Mississippi and Arkansas specs in
   `system.file("specs", package = "ReportR")` are complete examples.
2. **Prepare your data.** Load your records, run
   `standardize_student_results()`, then do your state's cleanup: recode
   subject codes and achievement-level labels to match the spec, set yes/no
   flags to `Yes`/`No`, and drop records that shouldn't be analyzed.
3. **Check the spec against the data.** Run `run_anomaly_analysis()` and read
   `$score_integrity`. Out-of-range scores or level mismatches point to a
   score range or cut score that needs fixing.
4. **Run, save, and render.** Run the lines you need, save each results list,
   and render the matching report templates.
